decisions.reason: SOL keeps both images and expresses their collision naturally.
SOL preserves the monsters’ blank staring and the sudden onset of darkness in clearer sentences.
“A force they could never have imagined” keeps the source’s sense of unimaginable power.
SOL keeps all three fear reactions and gives them brisk, parallel phrasing.
SOL changes the inability to cry out into an inability to cry out before death.
SOL drops the source’s point that the screams were erased as well as swallowed by the roar.
The source describes the aftermath of the collision; “the collision” itself changes the event.
SOL preserves the meteor image and makes the rhetorical question sound natural.
SOL keeps the fragments raining down on the statue-still monsters while clarifying the image.
SOL keeps the destruction-and-death image and the shuddering sky and earth.
“Everything mixed together” preserves the source’s image in natural English.
“Flee far enough” keeps the source’s point that escape was impossible.
“Barely hurt them” and “harder than alloy” retain the monsters’ durability.
“High-tier monsters” naturally conveys the category and retains their powerful magical power.
“Death bearing down on them” preserves the imminent threat.
SOL keeps the fighting-dog-and-tiger comparison and the point that greater strength prevails.
The source says the fragment flew in; SOL changes that action to striking.
“Open sky” keeps the Wyverns’ claim to the sky without changing the image.
The source specifies the shock wave reaching them; SOL replaces it with the less specific “force.”
“Stationed nearby” adds that the army was posted there; the source only says it was in the area.
SOL preserves the death wave’s scale and the point at which it began to subside.
SOL keeps the Dragon Lair’s destruction and renders the ruins aside naturally.
SOL preserves the overturned earth, mountain-like corpses, rivers of blood, and shaft of sunlight.
SOL retains this passage’s details in the preceding hunk rather than dropping them.
SOL drops the source’s emphasis on this particular moment.
“Parched lips” faithfully conveys the source’s dried-out lips.
“That was all” keeps the emphatic, brief close.
SOL keeps the clarification that he had no reason to care.
SOL retains the treasure’s greater value and fascination without the redundant comparison.
“A fitting price” preserves the idea of a price commensurate with what is gained.
The answer arriving before long keeps the source’s timing.
The source compares the hazy voice to a broken radio; “crackling” adds an unsupported sound.
SOL preserves the relief and the concern about Erasure while keeping the dialogue natural.
The source describes the shock wave caused by the collision; SOL recasts it as the force unleashed.
“Used all his power” preserves that Morgoth protected himself with everything he had.
“Ordained” adds a formal, quasi-divine sense not present in the source’s order of things.
BASE keeps the source’s comparison between drifting dust and the insignificance of the deaths.
SOL preserves that the being before him is his sole focus and objective.
SOL keeps his thanks and the Skeleton King’s surpassing his expectations.
The emphasis on “exceeded” is consistent with the passage’s stress on the word.
“Aimed at himself” keeps the opponent’s self-directed blow and the preparation for Erasure.
The italicized sound effect preserves the source’s taps and drips.
“Wet the ground at his feet” preserves where the liquid began to collect.
SOL keeps the molten-silver comparison and the blade through his palm.
SOL preserves that the pain stung all the more after a thousand years.
SOL retains the memory of his last pain and the greater humiliation that accompanied it.
SOL preserves the whispered name and Morgoth’s action of yanking free and seizing the sword.
SOL keeps both halves plunging into the ground and incorporates the owner’s reflected image.
SOL retains the reflection detail in the preceding hunk.
SOL preserves Morgoth bending toward and stroking the Skeleton King’s skull.
SOL keeps both things Morgoth urges him to accept: his origin and whom he belongs with.
“Like a hypnotic spell” conveys the source’s hypnotic comparison directly.
The Skeleton King’s refusal to waver remains clear without the redundant intensifier.
SOL keeps his failing consciousness and his effort to speak with his remaining strength.
The italics set off the remembered words without changing their meaning.
SOL drops the repeated “He’s the one,” losing the source’s emphasis on Jin as the person who did both things.
The source emphasizes that he was no longer alone because he was with everyone; SOL shifts the focus to their togetherness.
“Quit wasting your time” keeps the blunt dismissal and the same profanity.
The source describes the smile as both bright and radiant; SOL retains only brightness.
SOL drops the source’s sudden vanishing of the ghostly flames.
“Your friends” preserves Morgoth echoing the Skeleton King’s specific reference to his friends.
SOL keeps Morgoth pondering the words alone after the Skeleton King loses consciousness.
The source reflects on the singular word “friend”; SOL changes it to the plural.
SOL preserves the familiar-yet-strange feeling of hearing the word as if for the first time.
SOL keeps the years spent among humans and naturally renders his inability to understand friendship.
SOL preserves both questions about blood ties and people giving their lives for one another.
SOL drops the source’s explicit astonishment as well as fascination.
The source says “a human”; SOL’s “the human” makes the description definite.
“Among those” preserves Jin’s place among the people Morgoth watches carefully.
“Intensely curious” naturally conveys the newly added, powerful curiosity.
SOL keeps Morgoth looking out over the earth after the rumbling has stopped.
SOL preserves the sunlight, the Demon Realm comparison, and the land’s loss of magical power.
The short sentence keeps Morgoth’s indifference.
“Born of corruption” naturally preserves the source’s idea of magical power as corruption’s product.
“Or rather” preserves the correction that he had only been about to rouse his power.
SOL preserves the unexpectedness of the presence he sensed.
SOL keeps the magical power subsiding and the Black Dragon’s gaze sinking.
SOL retains the trembling air, still wind, and parting lips in brisk sentences.
“A guest had arrived” preserves his apology and the fact he had not sensed the visitor.
The source has the mist dispersing as he speaks in a low voice; SOL’s “quiet words” drops that vocal detail.
“Beyond it, someone answered” is the natural rendering of the source’s reply from beyond the mist.
“What’s that in your hand?” naturally preserves the question about what he is holding.
